extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for fiction writers on handling setting, manipulating pacing (time), using flashbacks, and choosing a narrative voice that suits point of view and story needs. Includes concrete rules of thumb, examples, and cautions for each element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of telling details
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember the importance of telling details, those tidbits of information that carry so much power in their little shells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillful use of telling details will allow you to convey your settings quickly, yet effectively. Example: instead of describing an entire shabby diner, focus on one antiquated dishwasher to make the reader feel present in the kitchen and allow the story to move onward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate descriptive 'space' to setting by importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself how important a particular time or place is to your story and this will help you determine how much 'space' to spend describing any given setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story takes place largely in one setting (e.g., 'The Fall of the House of Usher'), more description is warranted. If a character only briefly stops in a drugstore, you don't need pages of description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to omit setting when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a compelling reason not to describe your setting, then you have permission to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimalist authors (e.g., Raymond Carver) may include few specifics because the narrator isn't noting or interested in the surroundings. The lack of detail should make sense for the narrator and the story's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray real or seemingly real settings accurately and vividly
rubrics_metrics.description: Most fictional stories deal with authentic settings, portraying real places and times or at least seemingly real ones. Do your best to paint them accurately and vividly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you know the setting well, verify details; if you don't, gather information by visiting or researching (including online). Accurate detail aids verisimilitude and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictionalize unfamiliar locations to avoid factual errors and gain license
rubrics_metrics.description: If you're writing about a setting you don't know well, you may want to give it a fictional name so as not to do something like anger residents by mixing up street names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fictional place names (e.g., 'Leveland') free you from strict factual constraints and give dramatic license; they also let you calibrate details to the feel of the story (example: Beth Nugent's unnamed city).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend familiar with fabricated for semi-realistic settings
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find yourself creating settings that are only semirealistic, look for ways to blend the familiar with the fabricated to give your setting a sense of verisimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognizable sensory elements (posters, helicopters, familiar sights) placed in an unfamiliar framework to make an invented world feel internally accurate and believable (example: George Orwell's 1984).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop internal consistency for wholly fantastical worlds
rubrics_metrics.description: Even wholly fantastical settings should seem real and often demand more homework than other settings if you want them convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build mythology, history, geography, maps, and even languages as needed (Tolkien's extensive worldbuilding) so that the fantasy setting feels concrete and lived-in to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing as manipulation of time (compressing/expanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pacing refers to the manipulation of time—compressing and expanding it to fit the needs of your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer controls how quickly or slowly time flows: speed through irrelevant periods, slow down and expand the important sections. Proper pacing makes the narrative feel coherent and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace scenes according to their narrative importance
rubrics_metrics.description: If you move too quickly through an important section, the reader can feel disappointed or confused; if you move too slowly through irrelevant events, you can bore the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to how important your scene is to the overall story and pace it accordingly. Avoid dwelling on irrelevant events or skimming over pivotal ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow time in crisis via detailed scene work
rubrics_metrics.description: In moments of crisis, slow time down to reflect the character's experience, giving minute details and the panoply of thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing (as Toni Morrison does) with every awful thought and sensory detail is more effective than telling the reader the character 'felt' certain emotions. You may write several pages about several seconds; feel free to embellish if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate scene and summary to control pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the chief ways pacing is achieved is by alternating scene and summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summary to move quickly across spans of time (e.g., 'This blind man filled his ashtray and my wife emptied it.') and scenes to slow and dwell on important moments. Skillful alternation lets you cover hours believably in few pages (example: Raymond Carver's 'Cathedral').

rubrics_metrics.name: Let overall work length shape pacing choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Your pacing choices will be greatly affected by the length of your fictional work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In short stories you must be choosier about what you show; novellas and novels allow more space but still should exclude anything that doesn't significantly impact the tale. Plan how much time (and space) to spend on each part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flashbacks sparingly and anchor them clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Flashbacks are useful to relate events that occurred before the story's chosen timeframe, but they are usually better off not running too long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on flashbacks excessively—if you need pages of them, you may have started the story at the wrong point. Clearly delineate flashbacks and anchor them to the present to avoid confusing the reader; exceptions exist but require great skill (e.g., Beloved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice = the sound of the story; make it natural and unified
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice is what readers 'hear' in their heads when they're reading; it's the 'sound' of the story and the narrator that unifies a piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong work has one voice that leads the reader. The narrator's voice should sound natural, relaxed, and absorbed in telling so readers can be absorbed too. Focus on the narrator's voice for each individual piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose voice to match point of view and narrator personality
rubrics_metrics.description: More than anything else, your choice of voice is related to your point-of-view choice; a first-person narrator's voice must match that character's personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second- or third-person narrators are storytellers whose emotional distance affects voice. Consider how close or remote your narrator should be to the action when selecting voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational voice: features and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: The conversational voice feels like a casual conversation and is almost always in the first person, often employing colloquial speech and slang.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It lets first-person narrators go full throttle with personality (examples: Huck Finn, Holden Caulfield). The downside: it can sound like the narrator is blabbing intimate details for no reason—use with purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal voice: middle-of-the-road, adaptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal voice is not as casual as conversational but less dressed-up than formal; it often uses everyday language without overpowering personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works well in first or third person and can be close to a character's emotions while retaining some distance. It's commonly used in contemporary fiction and is a safe, flexible choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal voice: features, suitability, and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal voice conveys a degree of detachment from characters, is more 'dressed-up', and often suits sweeping, multi-generational or epic stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal voice is commonly third-person but can work in first-person if the narrator plausibly has a formal personality (e.g., Humbert Humbert). Beware of sounding like you're trying to 'sound like a writer' rather than a believable narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial voice: detached, lofty, or mock-detached tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial voice is lofty or mock-solemn and can be used to create distance or ironic commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although seemingly rare in fiction, it can be effective for sustained narratives where a detached, semi-joking chronicler voice helps the reader absorb bleak or epic material (example: Dickens' narrator in Oliver Twist).
